title: A System Prompt for K-12
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky reviews the 'STUDENTS FIRST Act,' a piece of model AI-in-schools legislation drafted by high schoolers in a three-day Senate simulation, using the metaphor of an AI 'system prompt' -- a document that constrains a system's behavior without changing its underlying architecture. He credits the students for genuine insight, particularly provisions requiring teacher transparency about AI use symmetrical to what's demanded of students, and procedural protections against false-positive AI-detection accusations, noting these reflect lived classroom experience largely absent from adult-written policy documents. The core of the piece is a prediction exercise: because 'system prompts get outranked' by later instructions, base defaults, and tool permissions, Potkalitsky forecasts which provisions will actually survive contact with real districts -- surveillance and detector requirements will stick because districts already own that infrastructure, while ambitious provisions like mandated pre-year student and family consultation will likely be overwritten because no district has built the capacity for genuine consultation. He closes by noting the document's fatal structural gap: unlike Anthropic's 'constitutional AI' approach, which builds a feedback loop where critiques of outputs revise the constitution itself, the Students First Act has no mechanism for the students who wrote it to learn what districts actually did with it or press for revisions.
points: Uses the 'system prompt' metaphor precisely: the student-drafted Act doesn't change any of school's underlying operating logic (grading, seat time, standardized assessment) -- it only reallocates what's permitted within those unchanged defaults.

Praises the students for including protections adults' policy documents typically miss, including symmetrical teacher-disclosure requirements and explicit procedural protection against AI-detector false positives.

Predicts specific provisions will fail to survive district implementation not from bad faith but from missing institutional capacity, contrasting detector/surveillance mandates (districts already own the infrastructure) with mandated pre-year student/family consultation (no district has ever built that process).

Identifies the document's core structural weakness by contrast with Anthropic's constitutional AI approach: there is no feedback loop letting the students who wrote the Act learn what districts did with it or press for revision.
quotes: The STUDENTS FIRST Act is this kind of text. Every provision reallocates permissions inside the existing operating logic of school. Grading, seat time, standardized assessment, discipline pathways, and credentialing all remain in place.

Students are watching teachers cede knowledge and agency to AI tools in ways that erode instruction and connection. They are receiving AI slop as instructional material. They saw a specific failure mode in the system they inhabit and wrote a mitigation into the prompt.
System prompts get outranked. Later instructions override them. Base model defaults override them. Tools with their own permissions override them.
The detector and lockdown browser requirements in Section 4.2 will survive. Districts already own the surveillance infrastructure.
No district has a process for genuine consultation, and none has an incentive to build one. Most districts finalize policy in August.

But the STUDENTS FIRST Act does not offer a clear pathway for creating such a loop. Interested districts will read it, engage with selected parts, ignore others, and the students who wrote it will have no way to learn what districts actually did or to press for revisions.
